Hi everyone,

For teams currently reaching 0.22 - 0.24 on the public leaderboard with single-agent configurations using gemma-4-31b-it-qat-w4a16-ct, I would appreciate community insights on a few architectural trade-offs:

1. Local Verification vs Global Clock Budget
In swegemma, running local targeted pytest suites (e.g., pytest -k with short tracebacks) allows catching simple regressions, but introduces command execution latency. Given the 12-hour global evaluation cap across the private benchmark repositories, have you found that running a local test and single repair loop provides a net positive on the final score, or does the overhead risk timeout starvation on heavier repositories?

2. Context Management under 32k Window
With thinking_budget set around 4096 and max_output_tokens at 8192, multi-turn trajectories (turns 10 to 15) consume significant context. What strategies are you using to prevent context overflow or losing the original issue specification late in the run? Are you strictly limiting shell outputs (e.g., piping to head/tail), or using structured state persistence?

3. First Edit Timing and Tool Budget Allocation
In an 8-minute / 28-call budget, what has proven to be the optimal window for applying the first source edit? Does forcing an early edit by call 8-10 yield better results, or is spending up to call 12 on root-cause analysis more reliable across unseen codebases?

4. Handling Sparse and Non-Standard Issue Prompts
Some benchmark tasks provide minimal context, such as a short title or an issue URL without reproduction snippets. Beyond inspecting recent repository commits via git log, what automated search heuristics have been effective for locating the relevant module without wasting exploration turns?

5. Repository Structure Edge Cases
Certain repositories test examples or tutorial code located in documentation directories rather than internal library modules. How does your agent differentiate between modifying core package internals versus documentation or example files?

Thanks in advance for sharing your thoughts and experiences.

text:
Our best single-model submission scores **0.949 public AUC**. We are sharing the accuracy recipe, our smaller 0.945 model for the efficiency track, and several changes that did not help.

The accuracy result uses one CoAtNet checkpoint trained at 384 pixels. At inference we take a native 320-pixel center crop and average probabilities from the original view and an anatomical left/right mirror. It is one learned model evaluated twice. The checkpoint itself averages three selected epochs from one training run, called SWA in our code.

## The score history

These are ordinary, full twelve-finding public leaderboard scores. Rows describe successive pipeline configurations; their differences are not all isolated causal effects.

| Configuration | Public AUC | Change |
|---|---:|---:|
| Our all-data CoAtNet, 80 slices and 78 windows | 0.939 | Starting point |
| 96 slices, native 384-pixel cache, 94 windows | 0.940 | +0.001 |
| Blend + JEV labels | 0.942 | +0.002 |
| Smaller 224-pixel crop model with epoch weight averaging | 0.940 | −0.002 |
| Add external OAI knee examples with masked labels | 0.945 | +0.005 |
| 384-pixel, full-field external-data recipe | 0.948 | +0.003 |
| Same weights, native 320-pixel inference crop | 0.948 | 0.000 |
| Same weights and crop, anatomical mirror probability averaging | **0.949** | **+0.001** |

The first density change also changed cached resolution and window count. Adding external examples increased training rows and optimizer updates, and the serving precision path changed. The 224-to-384 step also changed training crop geometry and the pretrained architecture variant. Those rows should be read as recipe comparisons rather than additive gains from individual factors.

## Training and labels

The model is a timm CoAtNet backbone with finding-specific multiple-instance attention pooling. We trained on 4,349 report-labeled competition studies; the 58 expert-labeled studies were excluded from training but reused for selection. The weak targets combine our report-derived soft labels with the public label sources credited below. In the external-data recipe, 2,399 OAI knees brought the training set to 6,748 rows. PF OA, Lateral OA and Synovitis received external supervision; unavailable finding cells were masked rather than treated as negatives. Positive class weights remained based on RSNA labels.

Both released candidates use seed 42, 16 epochs, backbone learning rate 4.01e−5, head learning rate 0.00195 and weight decay 0.0588. Training used 12 windows per study, batch size 1 and gradient accumulation over 16 studies; gold evaluation used 24 windows. The smaller model averages epochs 15, 13 and 12; the accuracy model averages epochs 14, 11 and 12. These selected averages are called SWA in our code. Adding external examples increased the scheduled optimizer updates from 4,336 to 6,736, so that comparison is not compute-matched.

## The final inference recipe

Each study has 96 preprocessed slices across five sagittal, coronal, and axial series slots. We evaluate 94 three-slice windows, process them in chunks of 16, and use finding-specific attention over the complete window bag.

For the accuracy model, native 384×384 windows are cropped to pixels `[32:352, 32:352]`. No resize is applied. Sagittal left/right mirroring reverses the three slice channels; coronal and axial mirroring flips image width. We use the center slice to determine the window plane and apply the transform before normalization. We average the two sigmoid probability vectors equally. The existing final per-finding percentile ranking preserves their ordering.

The smaller model uses a 307-pixel center crop resized to 224 pixels, the same 94-window policy, FP16 autocast, and one view. It scores 0.945. Recorded submit-to-score turnaround was about 7.2 minutes for that entry and 26.1 minutes for the mirrored accuracy entry. These include queueing and orchestration; they are **not official inference runtimes or efficiency ranks**.

## What did not help

| Tested change | Public AUC, reference → result |
|---|---:|
| Older model: 94 windows reduced to 24 | 0.940 → 0.934 |
| Older model: width-flip TTA across every imaging plane | 0.940 → 0.939 |
| Current weights: native crop reduced from 320 to 304 pixels | 0.948 → 0.947 |
| Current weights: native crop reduced from 320 to 288 pixels | 0.948 → 0.946 |
| Epoch 14 instead of averaged weights, same 320-pixel inference | 0.948 → 0.947 |
| Fresh training with corrected batch-normalization checkpoint replay | 0.948 → 0.944 |
| Fresh native 320-pixel crop training, anatomical mirror inference | 0.949 → 0.946 |

The all-plane width flip is different from anatomical mirroring, and it was tested on an older checkpoint. Its failure does not establish a controlled comparison between the mirror implementations. The new crop-trained model also failed to replace the incumbent despite encouraging gold diagnostics.

Our 58 labeled studies were reused for checkpoint selection and development. They are useful diagnostics, not independent cross-validation. For example, epoch 14 improved gold AUC while losing on the public board. Rounded public-score differences, especially +0.001, do not establish statistical significance or a private-test gain.

## Credits and release references

Thanks to [dreaddevelopment for the public Raptor CoAtNet/MIL recipe and baseline weights](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/dreaddevelopment/raptor-knee-widedense). That public checkpoint scored 0.924 in our baseline read; it is context, rather than a controlled starting point for the table. Our selected checkpoints were retrained. The public weak-label contributions include [stevenleehans](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/stevenleehans/rsna-knee-llm-report-labels), [pilkwang](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/pilkwang/rsna-knee-llm-labels), and [riadmohamed42's JEV labels and verification](https://www.kaggle.com/code/riadmohamed42/jev-knee-labels-verification). We thank RSNA and the competition data contributors.

Reproducibility notebooks: [accuracy, 0.949](https://www.kaggle.com/code/nartaa/rsna-knee-0949-anatomical-mirror) and [efficiency, 0.945](https://www.kaggle.com/code/nartaa/rsna-knee-0945-efficient-224crop). The [selected learned weights](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/nartaa/rsna-knee-publication-swa-weights-20261007) are a separate minimal dependency. Both notebooks preserve the exact scored scientific inference source and checkpoint hashes, include hardware/environment requirements, and are saved statically without running inference. No OAI images, identifiers, records, raw reports, subject-level labels or predictions are distributed.

Both models used the same 2,399 baseline OAI knees; the unsuccessful 12-month arm is excluded from these release models. The public Study describes aggregate methods/results while its exact-input linkage manifest remains restricted to qualified researchers.

Data and/or research tools used in the preparation of this manuscript were obtained and analyzed from the controlled access datasets distributed from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI), a data repository housed within the NIMH Data Archive (NDA). OAI is a collaborative informatics system created by the National Institute of Mental Health and the National Institute of Arthritis, Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS) to provide a worldwide resource to quicken the pace of biomarker identification, scientific investigation and OA drug development. Dataset identifier(s): 10.15154/0hcg-f676.

[Shared NDA Study](https://nda.nih.gov/study.html?id=3407) · [DOI: 10.15154/0hcg-f676](https://doi.org/10.15154/0hcg-f676). Official acknowledgement source: [NDA manuscript preparation](https://nda.nih.gov/nda/manuscript-preparation).

What worked for your models, and what looked promising locally but failed on the leaderboard? Please share useful negative results as well as improvements—especially experiences with weak labels, crop geometry, and plane-aware augmentation.

text:
Hi Kagglers! 👋

In synthetic tabular competitions like S6E10 (CTGAN-generated), the natural temptation is to **blindly expand features**—generating hundreds of interaction terms, target encodings, frequency tables, and statistical aggregations.

Inspired by several insightful discussions in our community, I conducted a **rigorous 5-fold scientific ablation study** across 4 popular candidate feature expansion modules (136 candidate features in total). The empirical results challenged standard intuition and exposed what we term the **"Feature Dilution Effect" in GBDT models**—blindly adding features actually degraded out-of-fold generalization!

Today, I am open-sourcing our complete, self-contained **15-fold GPU tree pipeline (Pure Standalone Tree Stack: Public LB 0.96114)**, and sharing how combining this clean baseline with external foundation models pushed our overall **OOF AUC to 0.96238**.

---

### 🙏 1. Standing on the Shoulders of Giants (Credits & Gratitude)

This work was made possible thanks to ideas shared openly by the community. Huge shout-out to:
- **@giannhsstamelias**: For discovering that in ordinal ratings, a score of `0` is **NOT** extreme dissatisfaction, but rather a structural **"Not Applicable / Unexperienced (N/A)"** flag.
- **@Shelton Wang**: For the inspiring breakdown of high-signal cross-domain interactions for CatBoost (`Class` / `Type of Travel` × Service Ratings).
- **@Sachith7**: For highlighting the immense value of using the uncorrupted original airline dataset as a Super Teacher prior.
- **@Chris Deotte**: For open-sourcing the incredible dataset of 11 Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) out-of-fold predictions.

---

### 🚨 2. The Great Ablation: Why 136 Candidate Features Hurt CV

Starting from a lean 84D baseline (LightGBM 5-Fold OOF AUC: `0.960262`), we independently evaluated 4 candidate expansion modules:

| Feature Expansion Module | Extra Dims | 5-Fold OOF AUC | Net Delta ($\Delta$ vs Base) | Conclusion |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Clean 84D Core** | **-** | **`0.960262`** | **Reference** | **Optimal Information Density** |
| `copy1_route` (Flight distance & rating residual routes) | +41 | `0.959788` | **-0.000474** 🔻 | Significant Drop |
| `copy2_org` (Original dataset marginal lookup tables) | +21 | `0.960093` | **-0.000169** 🔻 | Negative Contribution |
| `copy3_freq` (Category frequency encoding tables) | +42 | `0.960017` | **-0.000245** 🔻 | Negative Contribution |
| `copy4_digit` (Modulo math & first/last digit hashes) | +32 | `0.959896` | **-0.000366** 🔻 | Significant Drop |

Even when extracting standalone features with **univariate AUC > 0.80**, injecting them into the baseline still degraded the CV score.

**Why does this happen? (The Feature Dilution Effect)**
1. **Subsampling Dilution (`colsample_bytree = 0.7`)**: Trees sample a random subset of features for each tree. Redundant or noisy variants reduce the probability of selecting truly critical drivers (such as the `Super Teacher` score and key cross-interactions).
2. **Split Competition**: Decision trees make greedy splits. Correlated derivatives compete for split variance, splintering clean decision boundaries into fragmented sub-trees and causing subtle leaf-level overfitting.

**Engineering Decision**: We decisively **pruned all 136 candidate features** and eliminated 18 redundant baseline columns, locking our core feature space at **84 pure dimensions**.

---

### 💡 3. From Clean 15-Fold Tree Baseline (LB 0.96114) to Orthogonal Ensemble (OOF 0.96238)

Our solution architecture follows a two-stage strategy:

#### Stage 1: The Self-Contained 15-Fold GPU Tree Baseline (Open-Sourced Code)
- Built on the pruned 84D feature space (treating zeros as NaN for horizontal aggregates, cross-interactions, cognitive expectation gaps, and an uncorrupted Super Teacher prior).
- Scaled from 5-fold (80% train) to **15-fold (93.3% train, ~653k rows/fold)**.
- 15-fold parallel training on LightGBM + XGBoost + CatBoost drastically shrinks prediction variance.
- **Score**: Without blending any external public predictions, this pure tree stack hits **Public LB 0.96114**.

#### Stage 2: Orthogonal Fusion with Tabular Foundation Models
- Many high-scoring community blends (0.9618+) are heavy blends of shared public files that suffer from high mutual correlation ($\rho > 0.9999$).
- Because our 15-fold 84D tree model was trained strictly independently, its errors are **genuinely orthogonal** to neural/transformer representations.
- By stacking our 15-fold predictions with **@Chris Deotte's 11 Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs)** using an L2-regularized Logistic Regression ($C=0.003$) in logit space:
  $$z = \ln \left( \frac{p}{1 - p} \right)$$
  our overall ensemble OOF AUC surged to **`0.96238`**!

---

### 📦 Full Open-Source Reproducible Pipeline

The complete, end-to-end 15-fold GPU training and feature construction notebook is fully public and executable:  
👉 **[Notebook: Feature Engineering & Selection Deep Dive (LB 0.96114)](https://www.kaggle.com/code/jiatianzhang2/s6e10-15-fold-gpu-stacking-pipeline)**

Feel free to fork the code and inject these unpolluted tree predictions into your final ensemble for an orthogonal boost.

**If you found our ablation insights or 15-fold pipeline helpful, an upvote on the notebook and this discussion would be greatly appreciated!** 🚀

Let me know in the comments: Have you observed feature dilution in your experiments, and how do you handle feature selection on CTGAN synthetic data?

*5th place (gold) in [Kaggriculture](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture), team 有辣条有权.*

| Looking for | Go to |

| What we did, technique by technique, with links to the code | [HOW-IT-WORKS.md](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/HOW-IT-WORKS.md) |

| The code that matters, flat and grouped: features, Model 1, Model 2 | [code/](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/code) (Model 1 [`model.py`](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/code/model1/model.py), Model 2 [`nf_model.py`](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/code/model2/nf_model.py)) |
| Training on one replay, end to end | [quickstart/](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/quickstart) |
| How games were collected, filtered and sampled | [data/](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/data) |
| The submitted agents, and how candidates were compared | [submissions/](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/submissions) · [evaluation/](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/tree/main/evaluation) |
| Rebuilding both submissions from scratch | [REPRODUCE.md](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/REPRODUCE.md) |

## Intro

This covers my attempt at using SFT to solve Kaggriculture. It assumes the vocabulary in the [competition overview](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/kaggriculture/overview).

I don't quote leaderboard scores. The Elo-style rating only means something relative to the field at the time: a bot of the same strength would score several hundred points lower later on, because the field as a whole got stronger as time went on, and the rate of improvement increased closer to the deadline, especially once a lot of people moved to using all four quadrants in the last three days.

I mostly document what worked. Plenty didn't, and I don't keep meticulous logs of what failed. Each failure still cost real time. For example, I spent two weeks factoring the game's micro decisions into macro decisions, down to a page of theorems on how to handle them (311 claims, 919 linked pairs). This is the approach I really wanted to take, but it proved too much for agents to keep track of at once, even after I simplified it for them. They still made very subtle mistakes. I imagine this method will work once agents get stronger.

## Resources

I enter each competition to win or learn as much as possible, within a budget. Here: two 4090s I own, a 3090 (that kept dying), a DGX Spark and a laptop 4060 for eval games, Colab G4s rented on 29 and 30 Sep, and Kaggle CPU notebooks for evals. I have two Claude and two GPT subscriptions. These resources are shared among all my projects, including personal ones.

If I had more compute, I would have used it.

Team name: **有辣条有权** ("you la tiao you quan"). La tiao is a famous cheap spicy snack, and the name is a play on **有钱有权** ("you qian you quan"): "To have money is to have power." Swap 钱 (qian, money) for 辣条 (la tiao) and you get the team name.

## Models

These were my two final submissions. The larger, longer-trained B-even model finished ahead of N-flow and set the team's placing.

### Abandoned

The macro approach went first, so I won't discuss the architectures I considered there. Everything below came after I switched to micro decisions generated autoregressively. I had [this lecture series](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SQ3fZ1sAqXI&list=PLoROMvodv4rOY23Y0BoGoBGgQ1zmU_MT_) playing in the background, and it drove the switch. This game doesn't seem that different from writing a paragraph in a very specific style.

I train on the state the winner saw and the actions they sent. During play, the model generates worker commands, then orders, then STOP, one token at a time, with each token seeing the earlier choices from that turn.

Other failures:

1. **Chain of thought:** force an unsupervised label onto every tile before deciding.
2. **Recurrence in depth:** rerun the middle blocks several times. Showed a lot of promise early, with some of our best losses, but needed too many ablations to get right. No time to tune how many times, or which layers, to recur, and it ended up doing poorly late with the config I chose. Something I'll try earlier next time.
3. **Depth over width:** worse loss immediately.
4. **Massive parallel heads:** 36 heads of width 12. Did very well and only started to do poorly later, which leads to Model 1.

### Model 1: B-even

The 36-head model with its heads regrouped to 18 × 24. Shipped with a 4-update sprinkle on the five newest #1-team wins.

### Model 2: N flow

Random init on one G4. Shipped with a 15-min wash: low-learning-rate SFT on top-3 wins.

## Features

## Data

How the SFT data was filtered and changed:

- **Winners only.** Never imitate a losing action. In games we lost, train on the player who beat us.
- **Weighted to fresh and strong.** Hourly buckets by day and rank; the newest and strongest games get most of the draws.
- **Earlier, our own ladder games too.** Whatever beat our policy became training data.
- **Last day: top 3 only.** 30 Sep wins by the top three teams (404 source seats); the seats that beat #1 count 4x.
- **Short top-ups.** 15 minutes at low LR on the newest winners, exporting the current, unaveraged weights (RAW).
- **Held out.** Validation and sealed games were excluded early. Some validation games entered the late pool.

We could only find 3 wins against the first-place solution at the time we trained, and two of them were from its own validation games!

Replays came from Kaggle's daily episode dumps. The replay API was only for our own losses, and on the last two days for everything, at ~150-170 an hour. I also tried pulling replays by hand on the website: similar rate, but the API was less boring :D

## Biggest lesson

What I think was most useful was the workflow I refined during this competition, and will keep refining going forward.

Keep 2-3 ideas alive. Each has a fallback, a current best and a current experiment. Go crazy with the experiment until it beats the best, then try a new crazy experiment. Once you've experimented enough, the best becomes the new fallback. An experiment can itself be a set of ideas, so it's basically tree search over ideas.

Finally, we used a special version of the engine for matched games, so that shop rolls depend only on the initial seed.

## Code

Everything needed to rebuild both final submissions from the Kaggle episodes is in this repo. The episodes themselves are not included; they come from Kaggle. See [REPRODUCE.md](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/REPRODUCE.md). To jump from an idea in this write-up to the code that implements it, use [HOW-IT-WORKS.md](https://github.com/definitelynotrussellkirk-bit/kaggriculture-sft/blob/main/HOW-IT-WORKS.md).

# Q-FT: a Qwen transformer that reads tabular rows as embeddings

Kaggle Playground S6E10 (airline satisfaction, ROC AUC). How each row of the table is turned into vectors, fed into
Qwen3-0.6B, and trained; what LoRA does; and what we found.

**At a glance**
- **0.959795**: 5-fold OOF AUC, raw features only.
- **22**: positions per row (21 feature tokens + 1 CLS).
- **10.1M**: trainable LoRA parameters on a frozen 0.6B backbone.
- **~52 min**: per fold on one A100 (3 epochs, ~920 rows/s).

## 1. The idea in one picture

A language model normally reads *tokens* such as words. Q-FT skips text entirely:
1. It converts each **feature** of a row into one learned vector the same size as Qwen's word vectors (1,024 numbers).
2. It hands those vectors straight to Qwen.
3. It reads the answer from the last position.

It's the same trick vision-language models use for image patches.

## 2. How one feature becomes one token

Every one of the 21 columns gets its own small "embedder". Its output is the **sum** of up to three parts, then normalized to
the scale Qwen expects:

- **Column embedding**: says *which* column this is. It's initialized from Qwen's own word vectors for the column name (the
  mean of the vectors of the tokens in "Flight Distance"), then trained.
- **Value embedding**: a lookup table indexed by the feature's code. Each category, each rating level, each age, and each of
  3,300 Flight-Distance "routes" gets its own learned vector.
- **Numeric embedding** (Age, Flight Distance, both delays): the standardized number x goes through *periodic features*
  sin(2πf·x) and cos(2πf·x) at 32 learned frequencies f, then a small MLP (64 → 1,024). This is the same idea RealMLP uses so a
  network can resolve fine numeric differences.
- **RMSNorm × gain**: rescales the vector to RMS ≈ 0.030, the size of a typical Qwen word vector, so it enters the network like
  a normal token.

### How each column is coded

Vocabularies come from train + test features only (label-free).

| Columns | Value embedding (code) | Vocabulary | Numeric embedding |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Gender, Customer Type, Type of Travel, Class | category | 2, 2, 2, 3 | no |
| 13 service ratings (wifi … cleanliness) | rating level 0–5 | 6 each | no |
| Age | one code per distinct age | 75 | yes (standardized age) |
| Flight Distance | route id for every distance seen ≥ 3 times; rarer → "rare" code | 3,301 | yes (standardized log distance) |
| Departure / Arrival Delay | bucket {0, 1–5, 6–15, 16–30, 31–60, 61–120, >120, missing} | 8 each | yes (standardized log(1 + minutes)) |

Flight Distance gets both an ID and a number because in this dataset it behaves like a *route ID*: each distinct distance has
its own mix of passengers. The ID lets the model learn per-route effects; the number lets it share information between nearby
distances.

### Worked example: training row 0

| Column | Value | Code | Numeric x |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Gender | Female | 0 | – |
| Customer Type | Loyal Customer | 0 | – |
| Age | 36 | 29 | −0.217 |
| Type of Travel | Personal Travel | 1 | – |
| Class | Eco | 1 | – |
| Flight Distance | 694 | 436 | −0.594 |
| Inflight wifi / Time convenient / Online booking / Gate | 4 / 4 / 4 / 3 | 4 / 4 / 4 / 3 | – |
| Food / Online boarding / Seat comfort / Entertainment | 1 / 4 / 1 / 1 | 1 / 4 / 1 / 1 | – |
| On-board / Leg room / Baggage / Check-in / Cleanliness | 3 / 4 / 4 / 3 / 1 | 3 / 4 / 4 / 3 / 1 | – |
| Departure Delay / Arrival Delay | 0 / 0.0 | 0 / 0 | −0.289 / −0.281 |
| *Label* | *satisfaction = False* | target, never an input | |

These 21 codes and 4 numbers become 21 vectors of 1,024 numbers each, a 21 × 1,024 matrix that stands in for a "sentence".

## 3. Feeding the vectors into Qwen

Hugging Face models accept `inputs_embeds`: you can pass vectors directly instead of token ids, which skips Qwen's
word-embedding table. Q-FT builds the sequence like this:

1. **Shuffle the 21 feature tokens** into a fresh random order for every row, every training step.
2. **Append a learned CLS vector** as position 22. It's the model's "answer slot".
3. Qwen applies its usual rotary positions (0…21) and runs **causal attention**: each position sees only itself and earlier
   positions. So only the *last* position, CLS, sees all 21 features.
4. The final hidden state at CLS (1,024 numbers) goes through a `Linear(1024 → 1)` head, giving one logit.

> **Why the random order matters.** A causal transformer sees features one after another. With a fixed order, the model ties
> itself to that one sequence. Shuffling every row teaches it that order is meaningless (like a set) and acts as strong data
> augmentation. In our pilots the fixed order lost **0.0069 AUC** (0.9535 vs 0.9604).

## 4. LoRA: fine-tuning a big model by training a tiny add-on

Qwen3-0.6B has about 440M weights in its 28 layers. Instead of updating all of them, **LoRA** (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes
every original weight matrix W and learns a small correction next to it:

`output = W·x + (α / r) · B·(A·x)`

- **A** squeezes the input down to r = 16 numbers and **B** expands them back. Together B·A is a "rank-16" update to W.
- **B starts at zero**, so at step 0 the model is exactly pretrained Qwen. Training then moves only A and B. The scale
  α/r = 32/16 = 2.
- Adapters sit on all 7 projection matrices of every layer: attention q, k, v, o and MLP gate, up, down.
- **10.1M trainable LoRA weights** (about 2% of the backbone), plus 3.9M in the feature tokenizer and the CLS/head. The frozen
  0.6B weights still run in the forward and backward passes.

## 5. Training recipe

| Item | Setting |
|---|---|
| Data per fold | 559,708 outer-train rows (StratifiedKFold 5, seed 42); the held-out fold is only predicted |
| Backbone | Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-Base: 28 layers, width 1,024, 16 attention heads (8 key/value heads), MLP width 3,072 |
| Fine-tuning | LoRA rank 16 (α 32) on q/k/v/o/gate/up/down; backbone frozen otherwise |
| Loss | binary cross-entropy on the CLS logit |
| Optimizer | AdamW (fused). Learning rate 2e-4 for the LoRA adapters, 1e-3 for the tokenizer, CLS and head; no weight decay |
| Schedule | 3 epochs (3,279 steps of 512 rows), 3% linear warmup, then linear decay to 0 |
| Precision | bf16 autocast for the transformer, fp32 master weights; gradient clipping at 1.0 |
| Augmentation | new random feature order for every row at every step |
| Prediction | mean logit over 5 feature orders (the table's order + 4 random) |
| Cost | ~920 rows/s, 26 GB peak memory, ~52 min per fold on one A100 (5 folds in parallel on 5 GPUs) |

## 6. What we found

**Fold-0 pilots, 3 epochs each:**

| Variant | Fold-0 AUC | Takeaway |
|---|---:|---|
| **LoRA r16, pretrained Qwen** | **0.960444** | best |
| Random-init backbone (same architecture), full training | 0.960436 | pretraining adds nothing |
| Frozen backbone (only tokenizer + head train) | 0.959788 | a frozen LLM is already a decent feature mixer |
| Random column embeddings (no column names) | 0.958479 | names don't matter (compare full FT 0.958004) |
| Full fine-tune, learning rate 2e-5 | 0.958004 | learning rate too low for full FT |
| Fixed feature order | 0.953546 | shuffling is essential |

**All 5 folds:**

| Model | OOF AUC |
|---|---:|
| TabPFN-3.5 (raw features, fine-tuned) | 0.961248 |
| Kumo-Tabular Large (raw features, fine-tuned) | 0.960378 |
| **Q-FT, LoRA (raw features only)** | **0.959795** |
| Tuned XGBoost, raw features (8 seeds) | 0.959852 |
| Tuned RealMLP, raw features (8 seeds) | 0.959311 |

Q-FT folds: 0.959602 / 0.959070 / 0.960712 / 0.960388 / 0.959283.

## 7. Conclusion

- Our Tabular Transformer works great! On raw features it ties a tuned XGBoost and beats a tuned RealMLP. Wow!
- Next steps are to add tabular pretraining and in context learning similar to TFMs!

text:
Hi all! I'm currently at the top of the public LB (early days, it will move), and these are my notes from the **first two days**, for newcomers. Sections 1-4 need no extra data or GPU. Metric: balanced accuracy over 18 classes (chance about 0.056). Start with the [official getting-started thread + Discord (749382)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/749382).

**Pitfalls:** random K-fold, "cleaned" text, test-layout tricks that only work in CV, ignoring short passages, bf16 on T4, no internet at submission.

### 1. Group your folds by prompt

All 18 models answer each of the 150 train prompts once (2,699 rows; one prompt lacks one model). [Random vs grouped CV (749593)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/749593) showed random folds mislead (0.217 vs 0.369, LB 0.355), and my TF-IDF runs agree: only `StratifiedGroupKFold` with `groups=prompt_id` tracked the LB.

Why is random CV *pessimistic*? Training passages sharing a validation passage's topic all come from the other 17 models, so topic words pull predictions toward wrong labels. Grouped folds keep prompts unseen, like the test.

### 2. CPU baseline code

Char + word TF-IDF + logistic regression: **grouped CV 0.343 (the snippet below prints 0.3426 with sklearn 1.9.1), public LB 0.353**. Character-level details carry signal, so keep the text as given (`TfidfVectorizer` lowercases by default):

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy.sparse import hstack
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedGroupKFold
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score

tr = pd.read_csv('/kaggle/input/competitions/name-that-llm/train.csv')
y, oof = tr['model'].values, np.empty(len(tr), dtype=object)
cfgs = [dict(analyzer='char', ngram_range=(1, 5), max_features=300_000),
        dict(analyzer='word', ngram_range=(1, 2), max_features=200_000, token_pattern=r'(?u)\b\w+\b|[^\w\s]')]
cv = StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
for trn, val in cv.split(tr, y, groups=tr['prompt_id']):
    vs = [TfidfVectorizer(sublinear_tf=True, lowercase=False, min_df=2, **c) for c in cfgs]
    Xtr = hstack([v.fit_transform(tr.text.iloc[trn]) for v in vs]).tocsr()
    Xva = hstack([v.transform(tr.text.iloc[val]) for v in vs]).tocsr()
    oof[val] = LogisticRegression(C=10, max_iter=3000).fit(Xtr, y[trn]).predict(Xva)
print('grouped CV:', balanced_accuracy_score(y, oof))
```

Swap in `StratifiedKFold` to see the gap.

### 3. A trick that backfired

I clustered test passages into likely prompts and used Hungarian assignment (`scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment`) so each model appears at most once per cluster: **+~0.10** in grouped CV (up to 18 answers per prompt). On the public LB:

- plain TF-IDF: 0.353
- plus clustering + Hungarian: 0.344
- plus per-cluster log-prob centering (subtract the cluster mean per class): 0.329

One drop may be noise, but CV promised +0.10. My read: the hidden test likely has few passages per prompt; a CV that simulates the test is only as good as that guess. [Test-time grouping (750213)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/750213) also saw a smaller-than-simulated gain.

### 4. Short passages are hardest

Passages run ~40-250 words; short ones are much harder. Check your OOF by length:

```python
words = tr.text.str.split().str.len()
print(pd.Series(oof == y).groupby(pd.cut(words, [0, 60, 120, 180, 1000]), observed=True).mean())
```

### 5. Fine-tune an LLM (inference fits the free 2xT4)

With no extra data, Qwen3-14B-Base + LoRA r16 (all linear layers), a classification head, 3 epochs and `max_len` 384 gave **fold-0 CV 0.443, public LB 0.466** (TF-IDF: 0.353; public LoRA notebooks score higher). I trained outside Kaggle; inference on 2xT4:

- T4 has no bf16: use fp16. A 14B (~27.6 GiB) fits across both GPUs with `device_map="auto"` and ~14 GiB `max_memory` each.
- Merge LoRA into the base first (no peft overhead).
- Sort texts by length (max ~360 tokens, so 384 suffices): ~0.25 s/passage at batch 8, ~17-20 min for ~4,000 test rows.
- Attach weights as a Kaggle dataset.

### 6. Extra data: free options first

More passages from the 18 models help ([the generated-data debate (749447)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/749447)). Free, public sets: [18-model wide response corpus (749629)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/749629), [extra Claude passages (750224)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/750224), [helper dataset (750267)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/750267). Still open: rules on self-generated API data ([749613](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/749613)) and the Kaggle Benchmarks free quota ([750038](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/750038)).

Next read: [a beginner's journey from TF-IDF to LoRA notebooks (750230)](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/name-that-llm/discussion/750230). Thanks to all linked authors; questions and corrections welcome!
